purpose: The observation authority and its own query engine: immutable OBS# observation revisions, the per-scope accepted frontier and deletion fence, the accepted- and event-time segment directories, staged admission pages and their receipts, the durable spool and usage outbox, series claims and their cardinality counters, workspace ingest quota, the regional ingress gate, telemetry gaps, export state and export checkpoints. There is no downstream projection store and no change-feed rail: this table answers every supported query shape itself.

serverSideEncryption.rationale: Per-authority customer managed key. Observation rows carry customer log bodies and span attributes inline, so they may not share a key with any other authority.

globalSecondaryIndexes.name: gsi_scope_time
globalSecondaryIndexes.rationale: Scope-ordered event time on the canonical observation tuple. Only observation revisions carry tPk, so no control row, receipt or spool chunk can appear in a scope listing. The partition carries the signal, the event-time hour bucket and the shard, so a walk is a bounded range read per bucket rather than a scan. The bounded projection contains the wire decoder and indexed-filter fields; internal admission/accounting fields stay only in the authority row.

globalSecondaryIndexes.name: gsi_ws_accepted
globalSecondaryIndexes.rationale: Workspace-ordered accepted time on the canonical observation tuple; the stable observation id provides the unique cross-session tie-break without a shared counter. Same bounded projection as the other dense indexes: it contains the wire decoder and indexed-filter fields, while attrS, attrN, attrB and internal admission/accounting fields stay only in the authority row. A page that needs customer attributes issues a base-table BatchGetItem instead of tripling retained bytes.

globalSecondaryIndexes.name: gsi_ws_time
globalSecondaryIndexes.rationale: Workspace-ordered event time on the canonical observation tuple, the axis a dashboard reads. It is a separate index from the accepted-time one because a query may not silently answer an event-time question from an accepted-time order. Its bounded projection contains the wire decoder and indexed-filter fields; internal admission/accounting fields stay only in the authority row.

globalSecondaryIndexes.name: gsi_metric
globalSecondaryIndexes.rationale: One exact metric name inside one workspace per UTC day. KEYS_ONLY: an aggregate reads points from the base table under an explicit scan bound, so the index cannot become a second, unbounded copy of the series.

globalSecondaryIndexes.name: gsi_trace
globalSecondaryIndexes.rationale: One trace inside one scope, ordered by the canonical observation tuple. KEYS_ONLY: only spans and logs carrying a traceId appear, and the spans themselves are read by key from the base table.

globalSecondaryIndexes.name: gsi_control
globalSecondaryIndexes.rationale: The reconciler and the export launcher scan due work by domain shard and due time. KEYS_ONLY is what keeps the launcher's grant free of any observation read: a due page carries keys, and the launcher never sees a record.

globalSecondaryIndexes.name: gsi_gap
globalSecondaryIndexes.rationale: Workspace-scoped gap listing; a session-scoped gap query reads the base table by key. Only gap revisions carry gwPk, and the projection carries the gap's own fields and no observation field at all.

stream.rationale: A wake is a hint and carries no payload; KEYS_ONLY makes that structural, because there are no bytes to emit even by mistake. Frame bytes always come from a strongly consistent base-table range read at the socket's own durable position, so a missed, duplicated or reordered wake changes latency only.

timeToLive.rationale: Every reclaimable family here is reclaimed by a fenced reconciler duty that proves its own progress: batch.expire retires a preparing receipt past its deadline, spool.repair redrives an unacknowledged chunk, series.reclaim releases an idle claim against its counter in one transaction, and deletion.execute removes observations under a pinned deletion epoch. A TTL delete is unordered, unfenced and invisible to those duties, so it could remove a staged page mid-commit or a claim the counter still counts.
